planting.note: Set out container plants after all danger of frost, choosing a well-drained bed in full sun to light afternoon shade.

directions: This naturally occurring color break ripens pale yellow to apricot-orange instead of the typical scarlet red, giving a milder, less resinous flavor that many fresh-eating gardeners prefer over the standard red pitanga. It grows into the same dense, glossy-leaved shrub used for clipped hedges or patio specimens along the Gulf Coast, flowering and fruiting in flushes through the warm season once established. Keep it in well-drained soil and shelter young plants from hard freezes, since wood damage occurs once temperatures drop into the mid-20s Fahrenheit. Light hedge-trimming after a fruiting flush keeps plants compact and encourages the next round of bloom.

planting.note: Root cured pad cuttings in a lean, sharply drained bed in full sun; let cut pads callus in a dry shaded spot for one to two weeks before setting them in the ground.

directions: Named for the municipality in Hidalgo, Mexico where it has long been the leading commercial variety, this selection is grown specifically for its thin-skinned, white-fleshed tuna fruit, which is milder and less seedy than many other nopal cultivars. It roots readily from pad cuttings and tolerates drought and poor soil once settled in, but Gulf Coast humidity calls for raised, gritty beds and generous spacing between pads to keep air moving and limit fungal spotting. Harvest fruit in mid-to-late summer by twisting it free with tongs rather than bare hands, since the fine glochids on the fruit skin are far more irritating than the pad spines.
sources: FAO Cactus Pear (Opuntia spp.) Agro-Industrial Utilization Manual
